title: You're not hardcore, you're just an idiot.
summary: NH lists ten 'hardcore' gym behaviours spread by ego-driven social media that he sees as stupid: training through injury, extreme early rising, discomfort-as-recovery, puking on leg day, leg-day elitism, tearing calluses, ego lifting, fake-light 'range of motion' lifting, staying shredded year-round, and chain dips. Along the way he gives practical advice on recovery, callus care and how to load lifts.
claims: Fitness influencers keep reinventing the wheel to stay fresh, which often produces content worse than what existed before
Training through injury for status just aggravates it over and over; you never progress on an injury
A powerlifter he knew took painkillers to keep squatting through months of hip pain until his hip labrum tore
Injuries don't go away and get worse with age; tackled systematically with proper exercise selection, training is the best rehab
Waking at 3-5 am is pointless if you sleep the same amount; follow the schedule that suits you
During his master's he slept at 3-4 am because of teaching and coursework and still made tremendous gains
Any growth-hormone benefit from an early bedtime is minimal
Recovery means eating, sleeping and napping, not cold plunges or runs in the rain; nothing is more anabolic than a nap
He took only cold showers for 5 years and still made gains; they may have benefits but won't revolutionise your life or recovery
Constant 'active recovery' keeps you permanently fatigued; train hard, then actually rest
Puking during training means low work capacity, not a good session; if a set of 10 squats makes you vomit, improve your conditioning
Puke-inducing 30-rep squat circuits make the heart, lungs and stomach the limit instead of the muscles, and you lose the calories you need to grow
Leg-day elitism is silly; training legs heavy is a preference, and someone who only wants an upper body is entitled to it
Tearing calluses is not inevitable; he hasn't torn one in about 4 years after tearing them monthly
Shave calluses down with a nail clipper about every two months so the bar has no edge to tear
Rub a lotion bar (he likes Climb On) into calluses every night before bed, because chalk dries them out and makes them easier to tear
Everyone should lift heavy, but making it about ego leads to bad form that moves more weight while building less muscle
Optimal strength form and optimal bodybuilding form sit at opposite ends; good bodybuilding form with worse leverage and slower tempo means less weight
Ask how you can do a lift with as little weight as possible while challenging the muscle as much as possible
Lifting baby weight with pristine 'range of motion' form is also ego; a two-plate squat is not equal to a four-plate squat, and cheating lifters will outgrow you
Extreme range-of-motion and tempo methods have only worked, in his experience, for naturals maintaining a physique already built by other methods
Push yourself to add a rep or a bit more weight; a little ego helps progression
Staying shredded year-round keeps you in a catabolic state and stops growth; that is why some influencers look the same for five years
Very lean physiques mostly look good in photos; in real life these people look thin, and in the gym they are not impressive
'Fitness influencer syndrome': once successful, influencers stop growing and stay lean to look bigger on camera with lighting and pump
Chain dips with a 5-lb chain are pointless; master proper dips first, then load them with plates and a dip belt
exercises: do them properly, then load with plates and belt
chains around the neck add almost nothing
conditioning should not be the limit on hypertrophy sets
